GBR coral mortality: formal BRMS-BRT prediction models

Blocked validation, cross-fitted stacking, and all-event production refits

What was fitted

The response tables retain the established bleaching-attribution restriction: disturbance codes b, m, n, or an unrecorded disturbance are eligible, while records explicitly assigned to COTS, storms/cyclones, disease, or other excluded disturbances are not used. The meaning of m is unchanged, and blank disturbance records remain eligible when mortality can plausibly be attributed to the bleaching event. Genuine zero-loss observations are retained as controls.

The benchmark models remain interpretable references. They do not limit the production learners. The formal BRMS model is boundary-aware and hierarchical, with a nonlinear DHW response, all attainable environmental predictors, preceding-year Acropora proportion and absolute Acropora cover, a DHW–Acropora interaction, and prespecified DHW interactions with cloud, Secchi depth, current speed, prior severe heat exposure, ten-year cumulative heat load, signed thermal novelty, and an acute IMOS optical-extreme metric. Reef, event, and region effects capture repeated observations in the positive beta mean. Event and region effects are now also fitted in the zero-boundary component, where the earlier models most strongly underpredicted 2024 occurrence.

The BRT uses the same predictors in a two-part occurrence/magnitude model. Its positive component compares Gaussian mortality against a logit-Gaussian bounded response. Response scale, tree depth, learning rate, minimum node size, and tree number are selected only within each outer analysis fold.

All observations receive one out-of-fold prediction per validation scheme. Ensemble weights for a held-out fold are learned only from the other folds. Two ensembles are retained: a BRMS-BRT framework blend and a prediction-focused stack that may also use the low-variance benchmark. Final production weights use the event- and reef-blocked predictions; region blocking remains a geographic stress test. The final models are refitted on every modern event, including 2024.

Two prediction targets are kept explicit. Leave-one-event-out predictions are future-event forecasts and exclude event and region random effects. Reef-blocked predictions represent mapping an observed event to unsurveyed reefs and include the known event and region effects. Region-blocked predictions include the known event effect but exclude the held-out region effect. GBR-wide reconstruction should therefore be judged primarily from reef-blocked validation, while leave-one-event-out remains the stricter test of forecasting a new event.

Pre-event Acropora reconstruction

Acropora composition is aligned to the survey used as the pre-bleaching coral cover baseline. Exact reef, depth, and baseline-year observations are preferred. Where these are unavailable, only past observations are used: first the same reef, then a past-only spatial-temporal interpolation. No future community composition is allowed to enter a validation row.

Current predictive choice

The table below pools the two prespecified selection tasks: transfer to another event and transfer to unsurveyed reefs. It is an honest routing decision, not a claim that the winning learner is the most ecologically informative model.

Programme Learner n MAE RMSE Predictive R2 Balanced MAE Severe-event MAE Occurrence Brier Bias
LTMP benthic Benchmark-BRMS-BRT stack 398 0.082 0.126 0.433 0.085 0.234 0.232 -0.001
LTMP manta tow BRMS-BRT ensemble 496 0.095 0.129 0.294 0.099 0.195 0.221 -0.007
MMP inshore BRMS-BRT ensemble 180 0.166 0.233 -0.008 0.158 0.250 0.254 -0.022

RMSE remains the primary measure for the continuous expected-mortality target: it penalises large errors in the high-mortality observations that matter most for GBR-wide loss estimates. It is not sufficient alone for this zero-heavy response. Balanced MAE gives zero and positive observations equal influence, severe-event MAE targets observations with at least 20% mortality, and the occurrence Brier score assesses the boundary component.

LTMP and manta select the displayed routes consistently across the continuous error measures. MMP is less decisive: BRMS has the lowest pooled RMSE (0.231), but the BRMS–BRT ensemble is within 1%, improves balanced MAE and occurrence Brier score, and retains both modelling frameworks. It is therefore the provisional MMP production route. This explicit trade-off is preferable to declaring a DHW-only benchmark the winner from one metric in a small, three-event dataset.

Event context added in this refit

Ten-year cumulative load is the sum of annual DHW above 4 within the ten full calendar years before an event. Signed novelty is current annual maximum DHW minus the greatest annual maximum in that preceding window. Negative values therefore identify events weaker than recent exposure, while positive values identify unprecedented exposure. The acute optical predictor is 1.7 / Q90(Kd490) during January–March: lower values indicate unusually low water clarity. It is a consistent IMOS plume/turbidity proxy, not a direct salinity measurement.

Southern 2024 observations have positive mean novelty, including the Capricorn–Bunker signal, whereas 2022 is negative across the observed regions. Northern and central 2024 observations also have lower IMOS Secchi proxies than their 2022 counterparts. These summaries support the proposed mechanisms, but the optical metric cannot distinguish freshwater from sediment, coloured dissolved matter, or other sources of attenuation. Direct salinity remains a sensitivity analysis when a complete, consistent 2024 product is available.

For known-event reef-blocked reconstruction, BRMS reproduces 2024 mean mortality closely: 0.112 versus 0.113 observed for LTMP benthic, 0.171 versus 0.191 for manta tow, and 0.246 versus 0.238 for MMP. Occurrence is also close. Leave-one-event-out forecasting remains more conservative, particularly for MMP. The 2022 positive magnitude is still overpredicted by BRMS, although the known-event effect reduces the error. This residual is an explicit target for future event-mechanism work, not a reason to discard the bounded beta response.

Ensemble weights

The weights are performance estimates, not ecological importance measures. A weight near zero means that one learner did not add squared-error skill to the other under the current blocked data; it does not invalidate that framework’s uncertainty estimates or mechanistic interpretation.

Predictive influence

BRT influence measures predictive use, not causal effect or effect direction. Correlated thermal-history variables can share or exchange influence. The BRMS model therefore remains the appropriate framework for response-shape and uncertainty summaries, while blocked predictions decide production routing.

Ecological explanatory fit

Predictive validation and ecological explanation answer different questions. For the nested two-part GLM benchmarks, AICc and McFadden pseudo-R2 are reported for the binomial occurrence component. The positive-magnitude component is quasibinomial, so it has no likelihood-based AIC; its deviance explained is shown instead. The apparent response R2 is an in-sample descriptive statistic, not an estimate of transfer skill.

Adding preceding-year Acropora improves the apparent explanatory fit and the occurrence AICc in all three programmes. It does not uniformly improve blocked prediction in an unregularised GLM, especially for MMP. That combination is evidence of ecological signal plus overfitting risk, not evidence that Acropora should be removed. The predictor is therefore retained in the regularised BRT and BRMS learners.

Both Acropora measures are used by both BRT components. Absolute pre-event Acropora cover is particularly influential for occurrence in manta tow and MMP. Relative influence is predictive usage rather than a causal effect, and the two correlated composition measures may divide influence between them.

LTMP benthic 0.447 0.253 0.583 0.518 101.315 16 1.097

MMP inshore 0.284 0.071 0.507 0.387 47.252 7 0.870

Marginal Bayesian R2 describes the variance captured by the population-level environmental response; conditional Bayesian R2 also includes reef, event, and region effects. LOOIC is reported for completeness but is not used to compare programmes or route predictions. Each production fit has influential observations with Pareto k above 0.7, so these raw LOO values require moment matching or exact refits before they can support fine model comparisons.

AIC, LOOIC, and R2 are not interchangeable across the GLM, BRT, and BRMS frameworks. The models use different likelihoods and boundary constructions. Blocked scores on identical assessment rows remain the valid cross-framework comparison; model-family-specific fit statistics support interpretation within each framework.

Interpretation and next use

The formal comparison answers a predictive question: how well can each learner transfer to another bleaching event, another set of reefs, or another GBR region? Coefficients and variable influence are secondary and must be read in the context of correlated predictors. GBR-wide application should generate predictions from every saved full-data component and then apply the validated programme-specific route shown above. Environmental-novelty flags are still required for extrapolation checks even though signed novelty is now a fitted predictor, and BRT resampling uncertainty should be propagated alongside the BRMS posterior before publication.

IMOS MODIS-Aqua Kd490 is used consistently as the water-clarity source. It is preferred to the modelled eReefs chlorophyll/Kd490 field for this application and provides the required 2024 coverage. Recovered nearshore Secchi estimates retain their extraction radius and observation counts for sensitivity checks. The new acute optical metric uses the Q1 Kd490 90th percentile from the same source and extraction geometry; it should not be labelled freshwater exposure without independent salinity validation.
